thread.title: Stock Rally Fizzles in Wake of Strong Payrolls Report

title: Stock Rally Fizzles in Wake of Strong Payrolls Report
text:
Stock Rally Fizzles in Wake of Strong Payrolls Report By Nov. 2, 2018 7:33 p.m. ET Order Reprints Print Article Traders work the floor on the closing bell of the Dow Industrial Average at the New York Stock Exchange. Bryan R. Smith/AFP/Getty Images Text size
This is not the rally you’re looking for.
Yes, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 582.52 points, or 2.4%, to 25,270.83 last week, while the S & P 500 gained 2.4%, to 2723.06, and the Nasdaq Composite climbed 2.6%, to 7356.99. After a brutal October—the S & P 500 dropped 6.9%, its worst month since 2011—it was what we’d been hoping for.
Except not quite. It wasn’t just last Friday’s reversal, which saw the Dow turn a 198.24 point gain into a 109.91 point loss, though that certainly makes us uneasy. Nor was it the payroll data released on Friday, which confirms that the Federal Reserve will almost certainly be hiking rates in December. It wasn’t even Apple ’s (ticker: AAPL) 6.6% drop on Nov. 2, after providing weaker-than-expected guidance, which undermined a burgeoning tech rebound, or the progress/no progress comments on trade coming out of the White House.
Yes, all of those things mattered. But even before Friday, the market was not acting quite right. The S&P 500 gained 1.1% on Wednesday in what appeared to be a very good day. But the ratio of winning stocks to losers was just 3 to 2, which suggests that investors never seemed to buy into the rally. In fact, the difference between the two—118 net winners, according to FactSet data—was the fewest on a day where the market gained 1% or more since 2009, says Jonathan Krinsky, chief market technician at Bay Crest Partners. His conclusion seems spot on: “The probabilities that we head back lower from here has to now be elevated.”
There was a reason that investors never went all in on the rebound—they’d never capitulated in the first place. The CBOE Volatility Index, or VIX, traded only as high as 25.23 during the October selloff, well below February’s 37.23 peak, a sign that investors have been much more sanguine about the recent drop. Other measures that should have shown signs of capitulation—the ratio of downside trade volume versus upside volume—never rose to a level that suggests real fear, says Tim Hayes, chief global investment strategist at Ned Davis Research. And the fact that the market sold off so abruptly on Friday is just one more reason for investors to use rallies as opportunities to sell, rather than buy. “What you normally see is a waterfall decline that ultimately leads you into selling climax,” he says. “That’s been lacking here.” The firm cut its equity allocation to Underweight on Nov. 1, and now recommends that investors have half their portfolio in equities, 40% in bonds, and 10% in cash Newsletter Sign-up
That seems dire, but Hayes is quick to point out that he sees a pause in the long bull market, not an end. He compares the situation to 2011 and 2016, when worries about Europe’s debt crisis and problems in the U.S. oil patch, respectively, caused sharp pullbacks, but ended when investors realized no recession was imminent. “We will see that capitulation,” he says. “And it will be the start of a buying process.”
That could take a while. In 2011 and 2016, the S & P 500 suffered peak-to-trough declines around 19% before bouncing. The S & P 500 is 7.1% off its September high. ﻿
